standard_metadata.title: USGS & Cruden-Varnes Landslide Classification and Terminology Framework
primary_references: Highland, L.M., and Bobrowsky, P., 2008, The Landslide Handbook—A Guide to Understanding Landslides: U.S. Geological Survey Circular 1325, 129 p.

Cruden, D.M., and Varnes, D.J., 1996, Landslide Types and Processes, in Turner, A.K., and Schuster, R.L., eds., Landslides: Investigation and Mitigation: Transportation Research Board Special Report 247, National Academy of Sciences, p. 36-75.

Varnes, D.J., 1978, Slope Movement Types and Processes, in Schuster, R.L., and Krizek, R.J., eds., Landslides: Analysis and Control: Transportation Research Board Special Report 176, National Academy of Sciences, p. 11-33.
standard_metadata.organization: United States Geological Survey (USGS) & Transportation Research Board (TRB)

definitions.general_definition: A landslide is a general term used to describe the downslope movement of soil, rock, and organic materials under the effects of gravity and also the landform that results from such movement.
definitions.kinematic_definition: A downslope movement of rock or soil, or both, occurring on the surface of rupture—either curved (rotational slide) or planar (translational slide) rupture—in which much of the material often moves as a coherent or semicoherent mass with little internal deformation.

material_divisions.rock: A hard or firm mass that was intact and in its natural place before the initiation of movement.
material_divisions.soil: An aggregate of solid particles, generally of minerals and rocks, that either was transported or was formed by the weathering of rock in place. Subdivided into Earth and Debris.
material_divisions.earth: Soil in which 80% or more of the particles are smaller than 2 mm (sand-, silt-, and clay-sized particles).
material_divisions.debris: Soil containing a significant proportion of coarse fragments; 20% to 80% of the particles are greater than 2 mm in size (gravel, cobbles, and boulders).

Fall.definition: Detachment of soil or rock from a steep slope or cliff along a surface with little or no shear displacement; material descends primarily through the air by falling, bouncing, or rolling.
Fall.typical_velocity: Very Rapid to Extremely Rapid (Class 6-7, > 3 m/min to > 5 m/s)

Topple.definition: Forward rotation out of the slope of a mass of soil or rock about a point or axis below the center of gravity of the displaced mass.

Rotational Slide.definition: A slide in which the surface of rupture is curved concavely upward (spoon-shaped) and the slide movement is roughly rotational about an axis parallel to the ground surface.
Rotational Slide.typical_velocity: Slow to Moderate (Class 3-4, 1.6 m/yr to 1.8 m/h)

Translational Slide.definition: A landslide mass that moves out, or down and outward, along a relatively planar surface with little rotational movement or backward tilting; frequently controlled by structural discontinuities (bedding, joints, faults).
Translational Slide.typical_velocity: Moderate to Very Rapid (Class 4-6, 13 m/month to 5 m/s)

Lateral Spread.definition: Extension of a cohesive soil or rock mass combined with general subsidence of the fractured mass into softer underlying material; failure occurs by liquefaction or plastic flow.

Flow.definition: Spatially continuous movement in which shear surfaces are short-lived, closely spaced, and usually not preserved; component velocities resemble those in a viscous fluid.
Flow.typical_velocity: Rapid to Extremely Rapid (Class 5-7, 1.8 m/h to > 5 m/s)

Complex.definition: Slope failure involving a combination of two or more principal types of movement (e.g., Rock Slide evolving into a Debris Flow).

landslide_anatomy_features.crown: The practically undisplaced material still in place and adjacent to the highest parts of the main scarp.
landslide_anatomy_features.crown_cracks: Tension cracks in the crown that indicate incipient or retrogressive slope movement.
landslide_anatomy_features.main_scarp: A steep surface on the undisturbed ground at the upper edge of the landslide, caused by movement of the displaced mass away from undisturbed ground.
landslide_anatomy_features.minor_scarp: A steep surface on the displaced material produced by differential movements within the sliding mass.
landslide_anatomy_features.surface_of_rupture: The surface that forms the lower boundary of the displaced material below the original ground surface (shear plane).
landslide_anatomy_features.surface_of_separation: The part of the original ground surface now overlain by the foot of the landslide.
landslide_anatomy_features.head: The upper parts of the landslide along the contact between the displaced material and the main scarp.
landslide_anatomy_features.top: The highest point of contact between the displaced material and the main scarp.
landslide_anatomy_features.toe_of_surface_of_rupture: The intersection (usually buried) between the lower part of the surface of rupture and the original ground surface.
landslide_anatomy_features.toe: The lower, usually curved margin of the displaced material of a landslide, most distant from the main scarp.
landslide_anatomy_features.tip_of_toe: The point on the toe that is farthest from the top of the landslide.
landslide_anatomy_features.foot: The portion of the landslide that has moved beyond the toe of the surface of rupture and overlies the original ground surface.
landslide_anatomy_features.main_body: The part of the displaced material that overlies the surface of rupture between the main scarp and the toe of the surface of rupture.
landslide_anatomy_features.flanks: The undisplaced material adjacent to the sides of the rupture surface (described facing downslope from the crown).
landslide_anatomy_features.depleted_mass: The volume of the displaced material that overlies the rupture surface but underlies the original ground surface.
landslide_anatomy_features.accumulation: The volume of the displaced material that lies above the original ground surface.

Class_7.name: Extremely Rapid
Class_7.consequences: Catastrophe of major scale; buildings destroyed by impact; casualties high; evacuation impossible.

Class_6.name: Very Rapid
Class_6.consequences: Loss of life expected; some temporary evacuation possible; structures destroyed.

Class_5.name: Rapid
Class_5.consequences: Escape possible; property and structures destroyed; roads severely disrupted.

Class_4.name: Moderate
Class_4.consequences: Structures can be evacuated; temporary maintenance/repair feasible.

Class_3.name: Slow
Class_3.consequences: Remedial construction possible; structures may be maintained with ongoing repairs.

Class_2.name: Very Slow
Class_2.consequences: Imperceptible without optical or geotechnical instrumentation; structures crack slowly.

Class_1.name: Extremely Slow
Class_1.consequences: Imperceptible without long-term geodetic survey monitoring.

geological_causes: Weak, weathered, or fractured rock and soil materials
Adversely oriented structural discontinuities (faults, joints, bedding planes daylighting into cut face)
Contrast in permeability between permeable colluvial mantle and impermeable underlying bedrock
Contrast in stiffness (stiff fractured rock over plastic argillaceous strata)
morphological_causes: Fluvial or wave erosion undermining the slope toe
Tectonic or steep gravitational escarpment oversteepening
Deposition loading along the slope crest or upper bench
Vegetation stripping and loss of root cohesive reinforcement
physical_triggers: Prolonged antecedent precipitation and high-intensity storm rainfall
Transient perched groundwater table development and loss of matric suction
Hydrostatic cleft-water pressure build-up along open tension fissures
human_causes: Anthropogenic excavation / toe undercutting for roadway benching or foundation cuts
Surcharge loading at the slope crest (unengineered spoil disposal or building construction)
Defective hillside drainage causing concentrated runoff discharge into slope body
Deforestation, tree felling, and destabilizing agricultural terracing
